Arguments supporting the statement:
• Both traditions share Tawhid — the absolute belief in one God. Surah 112 is central to both.
• Both accept Muhammad as the Seal of the Prophets (Surah 33:40) and follow the Qur'an as the uncorrupted word of Allah.
• Both believe in a Day of Judgement and accountability. The Five Pillars are shared.

Arguments against:
• Shi'a belief includes Adalat (divine justice) as a separate root, emphasising Allah's fairness in a way the Sunni articles do not.
• The Imamate is a major theological difference — Shi'a Muslims believe in twelve infallible, divinely appointed Imams. Sunni Islam has no equivalent belief.
• Sunni belief lists angels and predestination as separate articles; Shi'a belief does not single them out as core roots.
• These differences lead to different sources of authority — Shi'a Muslims follow the teachings of the Imams alongside the Qur'an and Sunnah.
[12 marks]

Arguments supporting:
• The Qur'an is the direct, unchanged word of Allah — the only holy book that has not been corrupted. It is the supreme source of authority.
• It covers all aspects of life: worship, morality, law, family and social conduct.
• Surah 6:115 states: 'The word of your Lord has been fulfilled in truth and in justice' — suggesting the Qur'an is complete.

Arguments against:
• The Hadith and Sunnah are essential for understanding how to apply the Qur'an in practice. The Qur'an commands Muslims to pray but does not detail how — this comes from Muhammad's example.

• Scholarly consensus (ijma) and analogical reasoning (qiyas) are used to apply Qur'anic principles to modern issues not directly addressed in the text.
• The previous holy books (Torah, Psalms, Gospel) are also recognised as originally from Allah, even if Muslims believe they have been altered.

Arguments supporting:
• Akhirah gives purpose to this life — without belief in the afterlife, there would be less motivation to follow Allah's commands. This life is a test for the next.
• Surah 99:7–8 teaches that every deed, no matter how small, will be accounted for. This underpins all Muslim morality and worship.
• The Day of Judgement is when all other beliefs (Tawhid, prophethood, angels) culminate — it is the ultimate test of faith.

Arguments against:
• Tawhid (oneness of Allah) is the most fundamental belief — it is the first part of the Shahadah and the basis of all other beliefs. Without God, there would be no afterlife.
• Belief in the Qur'an and prophethood could be seen as more important because they provide the guidance Muslims need to pass the test of this life.
• All beliefs are interconnected — the Six Articles and Five Roots work as a complete system. Isolating one as 'most important' misses how they reinforce each other.
• Some Muslims might argue that practical obedience (the Five Pillars) matters more than any single doctrinal belief.
